headline: Wreck 2586 in 130 feet: sea bass to 4 pounds, yellowfin working the 200-foot break
subhead: Bluefin still showing on the Mud Hole lumps at first light, mahi stacking the lobster gear, and bonito starting to stage off Sea Girt ahead of the August 12 new moon.
body_markdown:
Wreck 2586 sits in 130 feet on the inside edge of the Mud Hole, and it's been in my book since 2011 as a sea bass wreck that never quits in early August. This week it proved it again — four- and five-man limits of black sea bass to 4 pounds, most of them coming off the up-current side of the structure on the last two hours of the incoming tide. Green crab and Gulp Grubs on 6-ounce sputniks got it done when the current was running hard; once it slacked off, guys switched to plain bucktails tipped with squid strips and kept picking at the bigger fish holding tight to the wreck's high spots. If you're running out of Manasquan or Belmar and want a sure thing before you commit to the long ride, this is where I'd start the day.

The bluefin have been more of a first-light proposition on the Mud Hole lumps — the 20-fathom humps on the east side, roughly 128 to 140 feet, where the bait's been holding tight since mid-July. Trolling spreads of small cedar plugs and green machines behind the boat at 6 to 7 knots have been drawing strikes right at gray light, and by 8 a.m. the window's usually closed. A few boats have had better luck switching to jigging — vertical work with 6-ounce Shimano Butterflies once they mark fish on the sounder holding 40 to 60 feet down over the lump. This isn't a stack-'em-up bite. It's two or three fish for the boats that put in the time and don't overrun the school with a second pass.

Farther out, the yellowfin bite is exactly what we called last week — the warm filament riding the canyon edges has tuna working temperature breaks and current seams in 200-plus feet of water, and the boats connecting are the ones running bait balls and working birds rather than blind-trolling. I had a report of yellowfin to 45 pounds coming off the edge inside the Triple Wrecks corridor, taken on a mix of trolled spreader bars and a chunk line once the boat found the right piece of structure holding bait under the birds. That thermocline everyone's been watching — bait and fish stacked in the 60- to 90-foot band under a hard temperature break — has held steady through this stretch of warm, settled weather, and there's no sign of it breaking down yet.

Mahi are doing what mahi do in August — they're on the pots. Lobster gear and high-flyers scattered across the Barnegat Ridge and out toward the deeper structure past the Klondike have been holding schoolies in the 2- to 4-pound range, with an occasional gaffer mixed in. The play is simple: idle up on the buoy, pitch a small chunk or a sabiki-caught bait off the stern, and let the school follow the boat before you commit lines. Don't blast in with the motor running — you'll spook the whole pod before you get a bait wet.

Bonito are still in a staging pattern rather than a full push, which tracks with what I'd expect this early in August. I've had a couple of scattered scout fish reported off Sea Girt Reef and along the edge of Shrewsbury Rocks, working bait pushed up against the reef structure in 60 to 70 feet, but it's not consistent enough yet to plan a trip around. The building tides heading into the August 12 new moon are the thing to watch — stronger current on that reef structure usually pulls the bonito and false albacore in tighter, and that's typically when the pattern goes from a curiosity to a real fishery. I'd keep half an eye on the Sea Girt and Shrewsbury numbers over the next ten days.

Blackfish and cod are off the table right now — both species want cooler water and tighter structure work that doesn't line up with an August pattern in this zone. I've got my tog spots marked and my rigs tied for the fall reopener, but there's no sense burning gas on Axel Carlson or the deeper wrecks for blackfish this week. Save that trip.

Wind's been the manageable kind — building sea breeze most afternoons out of the southwest, nothing that's shut down the fleet but enough that I've had guys moving their sea bass trips to the morning and saving the tuna run for when the breeze lays down closer to sunset. Worth building your day around if you're making the run past the 20-fathom line.

Looking at the week ahead, I'd expect the sea bass wrecks to keep producing at the same pace — that pattern's been remarkably stable through the warm stretch, and Wreck 2586 along with a couple of the numbers I've got marked near the Klondike edge should keep paying off on the same tide-and-bait combination. The tuna bite is the one I'm watching closest. If that canyon-adjacent filament holds its position through the week, the yellowfin bite over 200 feet should stay consistent for boats willing to run and work the birds. If it slides south or the thermocline breaks down under a cold front, I'd expect the fish to scatter and the Mud Hole lumps to become the more reliable bluefin bet again. Either way, I'd have my numbers ready for both scenarios before I leave the dock.
